sections.heading: Resting in Jesus’ care at the end of the day
sections.text:
Father, you love your people, and you have placed my whole life in Jesus’ hands. He is my Redeemer, my Lord, the one who loves me with faithful covenant love, and my friend. Thank you that you care for me in him.

Keep me close to him tonight. Make me holy in the way I live, harmless in the way I treat people, and clean from the stain of sin. Don’t let me be shaped by voices that do not belong to you. Teach me to know Jesus’ voice, to come to him where he is, and to follow wherever he leads.
theological_themes: Believers are held and cared for by the Father in and through Christ.
Christian holiness means belonging to Christ and being distinct from sin without becoming proud or withdrawn from people.
Jesus’ sheep learn his voice and follow his leading rather than the claims of false masters.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus describes his people as sheep who hear his voice, follow him, and are kept securely in his hand and the Father’s hand. This directly grounds the prayer’s trust in Christ’s care and the request to recognize and follow his voice.

The passage presents Jesus as the holy and undefiled High Priest who saves completely those who draw near to God through him. The prayer asks that the believer’s life increasingly reflect the purity and safety found first in Christ himself.

sections.heading: Asking to be washed from the day’s sin
sections.text:
You have washed me once for all through Jesus. My standing with you does not have to be rebuilt tonight. But I have still picked up the dirt of this day.

Please cleanse me from the sins I know about and the ones I barely noticed—from my failures, from the good I left undone, from the ways I went too far or not far enough. Wash my feet again, Lord Jesus. Be patient with me. Keep stooping down to deal gently with what is still wrong in me, and do not stop until your work in me is finished.
theological_themes: Christ’s once-for-all cleansing gives the believer a secure standing before God.
Daily confession remains necessary because believers still need cleansing from ongoing sin and weakness.
Jesus continues patiently sanctifying his people until his work in them is complete.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus distinguishes between being fully washed and still needing one’s feet washed, which fits the prayer’s distinction between once-for-all cleansing and daily cleansing from defilement.
John teaches believers to confess their sins, trusting God’s faithfulness and justice to forgive and cleanse. This supports the evening request for cleansing from the day’s sins and failures.
Paul’s confidence that God will complete the good work he began gives biblical ground for asking the Lord to continue patiently with the believer until sanctification is finished.

sections.heading: Fighting the sin that still clings to me
sections.text:
I want to be done with self-rule in every part of me. Help me put to death the desires that pull my body and heart away from you. Guard me from obvious, destructive sins, and also from the more polished sins that hide in my thoughts—pride, self-trust, clever excuses, and the need to be admired.

Let my whole life be for your glory. Make me able to keep going when criticism is unfair, and keep me from feeding on praise when people approve of me. I do not want other people’s opinions to become my master.
theological_themes: Sanctification includes an active fight against sinful desires, both obvious and subtle.
The believer’s body, mind, motives, and public reputation all belong under Christ’s lordship.
Living for God’s glory frees Christians from being controlled by either criticism or praise.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says believers put to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit. This supports the prayer’s desire to resist bodily desires and sinful self-rule, while depending on God rather than mere willpower.
Paul teaches that even ordinary actions are to be done for God’s glory. This grounds the prayer’s aim that the whole life, not only obviously religious acts, be directed toward God.
Paul contrasts serving Christ with living to please people. This helps frame the prayer’s request not to be ruled by either undeserved criticism or human praise.

sections.heading: Trusting the life your Spirit has given me
sections.text:
Thank you that the new life you have given me cannot be killed by what happens to me. My circumstances can trouble me, and my body can grow weak, but the life born from you belongs to you.

Nothing can finally undo the rule of your Spirit in me. Let it be enough for me to have your approval and a conscience that is clear before you.
theological_themes: The believer’s new life is secure because it comes from God and is kept by him.
The Holy Spirit’s indwelling presence establishes God’s rule within the believer.
A clear conscience before God matters more than outward reputation.

scripture_references.connection: Peter describes believers as born again to a living hope and guarded by God’s power through faith. This supports the prayer’s confidence that the new life God gives cannot ultimately be destroyed.
Paul teaches that the Spirit dwells in believers and gives life because of Christ. This illuminates the prayer’s confidence in the Spirit’s continuing dominion within the believer.
Paul makes pleasing the Lord his aim in light of final accountability before Christ. This supports the prayer’s desire to value God’s approval above human judgment.

sections.heading: Wanting to become like Jesus more than anything else
sections.text:
Keep me humble and dependent on you. Make me deeply joyful in you, calm and quiet like a child resting safely with a parent, and still serious and active in the work you give me.

I do not want to be impressive more than I want to be true. I do not want merely to do things for you while remaining unchanged. I want to become like Jesus.

If you make me right in the hidden places, then my life will be right. I belong to you, Lord. Make me into someone whose life fits the grace, holiness, and love of the One who owns me.
theological_themes: Christian maturity includes humility, dependence, quiet trust, joy, and active obedience.
Being formed into Christlikeness is deeper than outward productivity or religious activity.
Belonging to God leads to a life that increasingly reflects his character.

scripture_references.connection: David portrays humble trust as a weaned child quieted with its mother. This directly supports the prayer’s desire for calm dependence without passivity.

Jesus teaches that fruitfulness comes from abiding in him and that apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This grounds the prayer’s concern with being rightly rooted in Christ, not merely doing religious work.
Paul describes believers being transformed into the image of the Lord by the Spirit. This supports the prayer’s central longing to become like Jesus.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original applies language from Hebrews 7:26—“holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners”—which in context describes Christ as High Priest. The adaptation treats this as a prayer for reflected Christlike holiness, not as a claim that the believer becomes sinless or morally equal to Christ.

The phrase “Husband” reflects biblical bridal imagery for Christ and his people, but in contemporary individual prayer it can sound jarring or overly romanticized. The adaptation renders it as Christ’s faithful covenant love while preserving the substance of devoted, covenantal belonging.

The original’s “guard my manhood” is culturally and gender-bound language. Because the assigned voice is personal but not specifically male, the adaptation expresses the same concern as guarding the whole embodied life from obvious destructive sins.

The line about nothing hurting the “new-born inner man” could be misunderstood as denying real emotional, bodily, or circumstantial suffering. The adaptation clarifies that outward troubles can hurt, while the God-given new life cannot finally be destroyed.
The request to “exhibit a perfect character in Jesus” could imply perfectionism if isolated. The adaptation frames it as ongoing sanctification and increasing visibility of Jesus’ character.
significant_interpretive_choices: “This day’s defilement” was rendered as the dirt of the day, preserving the original’s connection to Jesus washing the disciples’ feet and the distinction between once-for-all cleansing and daily confession.
“Deficiencies of virtue” and “harmful extremes” were interpreted as sins of omission and imbalance—ways the believer either failed to do good or went beyond what was faithful and wise.
“The refined power of my natural mind” was interpreted as subtle intellectual or respectable forms of sin, such as pride, self-trust, and clever self-justification, rather than anti-intellectualism.
“I wish not so much to do as to be” was rendered as a desire for inward Christlikeness over mere outward productivity, while also preserving the original’s desire to remain “earnest and active.”
